page4_img_1.png.title: Bubble chart of anti-pattern frequency vs. impact
page4_img_1.png.description: A bubble plot relating how often Microsoft developers reported branch anti-patterns (x‑axis: Percent “Frequently”) to how much they judged them to harm productivity (y‑axis: Percent “High Impact”). Each orange bubble’s area encodes the product of frequency and severity, so larger bubbles indicate problems that are both common and highly harmful; the largest labeled bubble is Development Freeze (far right, high on y), indicating it is both frequent and judged highly impactful. Big Bang Merge appears near the top left (high impact but lower reported frequency), while Branchmania and Integration Wall sit toward the right‑center (moderate to high frequency and impact). Smaller numbered bubbles (5–13) cluster to the left and lower regions, indicating less combined frequency/severity for those anti‑patterns.

page5_img_2.png.title: Branch checkins: edits, anchors, and integrations
page5_img_2.png.description: A two-row schematic of a parent (bottom) and child (top) branch showing time flowing left-to-right and three kinds of checkins. Solid filled circles are edits (actual file changes), small hollow circles are anchors (temporal placeholders with no change) and large hollow circles are integrations (merge checkins). Arrows connect matching anchor and integration symbols to indicate the direction of a merge (parent→child or child→parent) and the diagram’s top bracket labels the three checkin types for easy reference. This visual encodes how the paper models branch histories and cross-branch merges when computing liveness and isolation.

page5_img_3.png.title: What‑if analysis: simulate branch removal to compare histories
page5_img_3.png.description: A simple schematic showing two stylized clouds labeled H0 (Original history) and H1 (Alternative history). A solid rightward arrow marked “(1) One or more branch removal operations” indicates creating H1 from H0 by removing branches; dotted return arrows labeled “(2) Compare liveness and isolation between H0 and H1” indicate the comparison step. The figure encapsulates the paper’s core method: replaying the recorded development history with simulated branch‑removal operations to produce an alternative history, then measuring changes in liveness (transit time / delay) and isolation (conflicts avoided) between H0 and H1 to quantify branch cost and benefit.

page2_img_2.png.title: Survey questions on branching and integration effort
page2_img_2.png.description: A screenshot of the survey instrument (Figure 2) listing the five branching-related questions used in the study (Q1–Q6). Q1 asks for a numeric estimate (hours per month spent creating branches and integrating changes); Q2–Q4 are open comment prompts about average integration time (with units), how integration correctness is validated, and errors caused by incorrect integrations. Q5 asks how often the respondent has encountered a set of branch anti‑patterns (referencing Appleton et al.) with the ordinal choices Never | Once or twice | Occasionally | Frequently | No opinion, and Q6 asks the perceived impact of those anti‑patterns on productivity with choices No impact | Small impact | Moderate impact | Large impact | No opinion.

page3_img_1.png.title: Branch anti-patterns with brief one-line definitions
page3_img_1.png.description: A vertically arranged list of 13 branch ‘anti‑patterns’ each paired with a one‑line definition (e.g., “Merge Paranoia — avoiding merging at all cost,” “Merge Mania — spending too much time merging,” “Big Bang Merge — deferring merges and attempting to merge all branches simultaneously,” “Branch Mania — creating too many branches,” and “Spaghetti Branching — integrating changes between unrelated branches”). The figure enumerates common problematic branching practices identified by Appleton et al. and used as the survey items in this study. These named anti‑patterns were later analyzed for frequency and impact in the paper (with Development Freeze, Big Bang Merge, Integration Wall, and Branchmania emerging as the highest combined frequency/severity).

page8_img_1.png.title: Branch isolation vs. delay scatterplot (sheep, hybrid, goat clusters)
page8_img_1.png.description: A scatterplot that compares normalized isolation (x‑axis; farther right = more conflicts prevented) against normalized delay (y‑axis; lower = less delay) for individual Windows branches under a recursive branch‑removal scenario. Each point is a branch and points are colored by category: red (goats) clustered at top‑left indicating low isolation but high delay, blue (hybrids) in the middle, and green (sheep) at bottom‑right indicating high isolation with low delay. The figure includes group regression/threshold lines (solid and dashed) that visualize the tradeoff between preventing conflicts and incurring delay; branches were categorized by ranking isolation and delay (bottom 25% = sheep, middle 50% = hybrids, top 25% = goats). This visualization was used in the paper to identify high‑cost/low‑benefit branches that are candidates for removal or refactoring.

page8_img_2.png.title: Days saved and conflicts added per edit for branch-removal strategies
page8_img_2.png.description: The table lists average outcomes per edit for three branch-removal strategies: removing ‘Sheep’, removing ‘Goats’, and an ideal ‘Optimal’ choice. Removing goat branches would have saved 8.9 days of delay per edit while introducing 0.042 additional conflicts per edit; removing sheep branches saves only 2.3 days but adds 0.218 conflicts per edit. The optimal (perfect-foresight) choice would save 9.7 days and add 0.035 conflicts, so the goat-based selection (made from mid-cycle data) achieves about 92% of the maximum delay reduction while incurring only a small extra conflict rate versus the optimum.

page9_img_1.png.title: Effect of maximum branch depth on transit time decrease and edits in conflict
page9_img_1.png.description: The table shows, for maximum branch depths 0–4, the percent decrease in total transit time (how much faster edits would reach the root) and the percent of edits that would be in conflict (loss of isolation) if the branch hierarchy were limited to that depth. At depth 0 (no branches) transit time falls by 100% but 41.0% of edits would be in conflict; at depth 1 transit time decreases by 8.9% with 30.3% of edits conflicting. Further relaxing depth yields rapidly diminishing benefits: depth 2 = 3.4% time decrease and 10.5% conflicts; depth 3 = 1.4% and 2.3%; depth 4 = <0.1% and 0.2%. The numbers illustrate the paper’s point that removing deep branches has minimal impact on liveness, whereas meaningful speedups require very shallow branching at the cost of many more conflicting edits.

page5_img_1.png.title: Simulation steps for removing a victim branch (A parent, B victim)
page5_img_1.png.description: Four-panel schematic that shows how the authors simulate removing a child (victim) branch B and folding its activity into its parent A to produce an alternative history H1. Panel (a) (H0) shows two parallel timelines for A and B with solid circles denoting edits and hollow circles denoting integrations/anchors (time flows left to right). Panel (b) moves the checkins originally made on B (colored orange) onto A while preserving chronological order; panel (c) deletes the now-redundant integrations between parent and victim; panel (d) shows the final alternative history H1 where all edits reside on A and former integrations have been removed or rerouted. This visualization summarizes the edit relocation and integration-removal steps used to measure the change in transit time (delay) and the conflicts introduced (isolation) when a branch is removed.

page6_img_1.png.title: Simulated branch removal showing moved edits, removed integrations, and new conflicts
page6_img_1.png.description: The figure is a two-row diagram comparing (a) the original development history and (b) the alternative history produced when the middle (victim) branch is removed. Three horizontal lines are shown: Child Branch (top, green edits), Victim Branch (middle, orange edits), and Parent Branch (bottom, blue edits); solid circles are edits, hollow circles are integration/anchor checkins, and specific checkins are labeled a–f while integrations marked x and y are removed. After removing the victim branch, its edits are moved onto the parent, two integrations (x and y) are eliminated and integrations to children are rerouted, which shortens the transit path for child edits e and f but creates several sequential edit pairs on the parent that become potential conflicts (five introduced, indicated by arcs). The illustration concretely demonstrates the paper’s trade-off: branch removal can improve liveness (faster transit) for some edits while reducing isolation (introducing new conflicts) for others.

page2_img_1.png.title: Hierarchical Windows branch structure with forward and reverse integrations
page2_img_1.png.description: A three-level schematic of the Windows branching hierarchy: Main Branch (Level 0) at the bottom, Multiple Area Branches (Level 1), Multiple Component Branches (Level 2), and Feature Branches along the top. Black arrows on the top line mark developer check-ins made on feature branches. Vertical arrows labelled “FI” point upward from parent lines to child lines to indicate forward integrations (parent→child) used to keep child/feature branches up to date, while downward arrows labelled “RI” indicate reverse integrations (child→parent) that propagate completed changes back toward the main branch. The figure illustrates the directional flow of edits and integrations that the paper later measures as transit time (liveness) and conflict prevention (isolation).
